lead.headline: Vienna Roman mass grave dated to late 1st-early 2nd century CE; 85% of injuries perimortem
lead.summary: Beneath a Vienna soccer field, the first known Roman mass war grave yielded 129 male skeletons.
facts: 129 male skeletons, all but two of them men aged 20 to 30
85% of the recorded injuries happened at or around the time of death
Radiocarbon and coin finds place the burial between 80 and 130 CE
lead.post_text:
Renovation work under a soccer pitch in Vienna-Simmering hit a pit packed with human bone, and the excavation that followed found 129 skeletons laid down in a single event.
Almost all are men between 20 and 30, and 85% of the injuries — blade cuts, lance punctures, blunt trauma — happened at or around the time of death.
That combination makes it the first Roman mass war grave known from Central Europe. https://www.wien.gv.at/kultur/archaeologie/simmering/
lead.video_title: Rome's Lost Battle Under a Soccer Field

web_sources.snippet: The pit held 129 individuals in a single depositional event.

web_sources.snippet: Blade and lance injuries dominate the recorded trauma.

rail.headline: 1-million-year-old stone tools on Sulawesi suggest earliest known seafaring
rail.summary: Seven stone flakes found in a Sulawesi cornfield may date to 1.04 to 1.48 million years old.
facts: Seven flakes recovered from the Calio site on Sulawesi
Bracketed between 1.04 and 1.48 million years old
rail.post_text:
Seven sharp-edged flakes came out of a cornfield at Calio in South Sulawesi, sealed in a layer that dates between 1.04 and 1.48 million years.
Sulawesi has never been connected to the mainland, so whoever knapped them crossed open water to get there.
rail.video_title: Who Crossed to Sulawesi a Million Years Ago?

web_sources.title: Early hominin presence on Sulawesi
web_sources.snippet: The Calio flakes predate every other artefact known from Wallacea.

rail.headline: DNA confirms Mississippian cacao consumption at Etowah, Georgia, around 1000 years ago
rail.summary: Genetic sequencing confirmed cacao DNA on 11th to 12th century pottery shards from Etowah.
facts: Cacao DNA recovered from residue on 11th-century sherds
rail.post_text:
Residue scraped from Etowah pottery carried cacao DNA, and the sherds themselves date to the 11th and 12th centuries.
The nearest cacao grows some 2,000 kilometres south, which puts Etowah on a trade route nobody had mapped that far north.

lead.title: Week of August 31: 476,000-Year-Old Wooden Structure Found, Dire Wolf Pups Born, and More
lead.summary: Archaeologists at Kalambo Falls uncovered the oldest known wooden structure.
lead.body_html:
Artifact Discoveries

Archaeologists at Kalambo Falls in Zambia reported two interlocking logs, shaped with stone tools and preserved in waterlogged sand, that push the oldest known wooden structure back to about 476,000 years ago.

The find predates Homo sapiens, so whoever cut that notch was not us — which makes the carpentry, not the wood, the headline.

lead.title: The Egyptian Hard-Stone Precision Debate
lead.summary: Mainstream explanations of Egyptian hard-stone working are tested against the Serapeum boxes.
lead.body_html: The Serapeum boxes are the strongest single test of the mainstream account: 27 granite chests, each cut to tolerances that copper tools and sand abrasives are not obviously able to hold.
